related_questions.question: How do I find all my 401k money?

text_blocks.snippet: To find your 401(k) money, start by contacting your former employers or their plan administrators to inquire about your account details and options. You can also search for unclaimed retirement benefits through National Registry of Unclaimed Retirement Benefits or your state's unclaimed property database.

list.title: 1. Contact your former employers:
list.snippet: Reach out to the HR or benefits department of your past employers and inquire about your 401(k) plan. Provide them with necessary details like your name, Social Security number, and employment dates.

list.title: 2. Check old statements:
list.snippet: Review any old 401(k) statements you might have. They often contain contact information for the plan administrator.

National Registry of Unclaimed Retirement Benefits: This database allows you to search for unclaimed retirement funds, including 401(k)s, using your Social Security number, according to Bankrate and Fidelity.
State unclaimed property databases: Many states have online databases where you can search for unclaimed property, including retirement funds.
U.S. Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration (EBSA): They offer tools and resources for locating lost retirement plans.

list.title: 4. Consider professional help:
list.snippet: If you're still having trouble, consider consulting with a financial advisor or retirement specialist for assistance.

related_questions.question: What happens to your 401k when you quit?

text_blocks.snippet: When you quit your job, your 401(k) doesn't disappear. You have several options for what to do with it, including leaving it with your former employer, rolling it over into a new employer's plan or an IRA, or taking a lump-sum distribution (which may have tax implications).
Here's a breakdown of the common scenarios:

list.title: Leaving it with your former employer:
list.snippet: You can keep your 401(k) with your previous employer, but you'll no longer be able to contribute to it.

list.title: Rolling it over:
list.snippet: You can transfer your 401(k) balance to a new employer's plan (if they accept rollovers) or to a traditional or Roth IRA.

list.title: Cashing out:
list.snippet: You can withdraw the money, but you'll likely face taxes and penalties, especially if you're under 59 1/2.

list.title: Vesting:
list.snippet: Make sure you understand your vesting schedule. Employer contributions may not be fully yours until you've worked for a certain period.

list.title: Fees:
list.snippet: Be aware of any fees associated with your 401(k), as they may increase after you leave your job.

list.title: Rollover Options:
list.snippet: Consider whether rolling over to an IRA or a new employer's plan is the best option for you based on your financial situation and future goals.
